newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel tough on EMU targets despite budget woes.
newsitem.headline: Waigel tough on EMU targets despite budget woes.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel demanded strict interpretation of the criteria for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) on Thursday despite mounting budget problems casting a shadow over German eligibility for it.

Waigel, speaking only hours before a tax revenue estimate was expected to tear another gaping hole in his budget, said adherence to the strict Maastricht criteria would determine which European Union countries launch the euro in 1999.

He was speaking in a parliamentary debate which ended with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's majority defeating an opposition motion calling for an active jobs policy to be included in the "stability pact" meant to guarantee the euro's value.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) threatened to reject the revised version of the Maastricht treaty due to be approved at the EU's Amsterdam summit in June if it did not include an active European jobs policy.

But speakers from the SPD and ecologist Greens party also strongly supported the euro, arguing that a stable single currency was urgently needed to support German exports and help the EU avoid the worst effects of currency speculation.

Strategists for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said they considered the SPD threat a tactical move and did not expect the strongly pro-European party to waver when parliamentary approval is needed to join EMU.
"I will oppose any softening of the criteria," said Waigel, who on Wednesday said he was considering stop-gap measures to make up for a huge expected shortfall in tax revenues.
An expert committee was due to announce later on Thursday the full extent of the shortfall, which government officials say should be about 20 billion marks.
Waigel admitted on Wednesday the federal deficit would widen this year because record jobless levels triggered higher unemployment payments that he could not control.

He said Bonn's deficit might have to widen this year, the crucial year for keeping under the Maastricht deficit ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), but Germany would still be within the limits for 1997.

The finance minister, who did not mention his budget problems in his speech, stressed the Maastricht criteria more than the 1999 starting date, which the SPD said must be kept to avoid a major setback to European integration.

"Not all 15 EU member states will be able to or want to fulfil the strict demands of the (Maastricht) treaty and the stability pact," he said. "Convergence determines the timetable, for every country."

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, from the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP), said he was firmly against any delay: "The euro is needed on time if we do not want to damage the single market."
The SPD criticism was strongly pro-European, with several speakers criticising the government for not doing enough to rally support for the euro among a sceptical population.
Over two-thirds of all Germans oppose giving up the mark, but few politicians have tried to tap this feeling with a Euro-sceptical campaign that could be seen as overtly nationalistic.
Meanwhile, speculation mounted about how Waigel would find more funds to fill the gap the tax shortfall would create.

His ministry denied a report in the Handelsblatt business daily that some members of Kohl's coalition wanted to sell Bundesbank gold reserves to avert tax increases. Coalition sources have told Reuters Waigel plans to discuss revaluing Germany's gold reserves with the Bundesbank but not selling them.
Handelsblatt said the Bundesbank holds 95 million ounces in gold reserves that were originally acquired at an average price of 144 marks an ounce, for a total value of 13.7 billion marks.
At the current market value of about 600 marks an ounce, the gold would be worth about 57 billion marks, it said.

German newspapers on Thursday attacked Waigel for failing to prepare for the widening gap in German public finances and were particularly critical of the idea of selling some of Bonn's holdings in the telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom.

"Theo Waigel is behaving like someone who has hit on hard times. After a quick look in the piggy bank, off he rushes to the flea market to sell the first thing of value he can lay his hands on," said the Frankfurter Rundschau.
